title: Trump: J.D. Vance says Peter Thiel’s Yale talk shaped his thinking
description_medium: At Yale Law School in 2011, J.D. Vance attended a talk by investor Peter Thiel. In a 2020 essay, Vance called it the most significant moment of his time at Yale and said it articulated a feeling he had not previously been able to express. He later described how the encounter affected his thinking, while the timeline says the two became friends and collaborators.
description_long: J.D. Vance met investor Peter Thiel while studying at Yale Law School in 2011. Thiel spoke to students about the pressure to compete for increasingly prestigious jobs and argued that professional status could come at the expense of meaningful work. In a 2020 first-person essay, Vance called the talk the most significant moment of his time at Yale. He wrote that Thiel’s argument helped him recognize how strongly he had pursued achievement as a social competition rather than for a purpose he understood. Vance said the talk prompted him to reconsider a legal career; he also described Thiel’s Christianity as challenging his assumptions about faith and intelligence. The essay places the encounter within Vance’s later turn toward Catholicism, but it presents a personal reflection rather than a full account of the speech’s influence on his political views. The timeline records that the two later became friends and collaborators. That relationship and Vance’s own account support calling the talk formative in his intellectual development, without treating it as proof of any particular later political motive.

title: Trump: New York files a fraud lawsuit against Trump University
description_medium: In 2013, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman sued Donald Trump, Trump University, and its former president, alleging persistent fraud and deceptive business practices. The state said the program misrepresented its instruction and instructors and sought $40 million. Those were allegations in a civil case, not criminal charges or a finding that Trump committed fraud.
description_long: In 2013, New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman filed a civil lawsuit against Donald Trump, Trump University, and the program’s former president. The state alleged that Trump University misled customers about the quality of its real-estate instruction, its instructors, and the help students would receive. Schneiderman said the business had operated without required licensing and accused it of persistent fraud and deceptive practices. The state sought $40 million in restitution and penalties. Trump’s lawyer denied that the venture defrauded students and called the lawsuit false. The filing placed the business’s sales claims and seminar practices before a state court, but the allegations were contested and the complaint itself was not a finding of liability or a criminal conviction. The case formed part of a broader dispute over consumers who said they paid substantial sums for training that did not deliver the promised instruction or opportunities. The event is the state’s decision to sue and the claims it made at that point; later court proceedings and settlement terms are separate developments.

title: Trump Foundation made an illegal $25,000 contribution linked to Pam Bondi
description_medium: In 2013, the Trump Foundation made a $25,000 payment to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi while her office was considering complaints about Trump University. The foundation later corrected its tax filing and paid a $2,500 penalty. The Washington Post reported that the foundation acknowledged an illegal political contribution; the timing does not by itself establish a bribe or an exchange for official action.
description_long: The Donald J. Trump Foundation paid $25,000 in 2013 to a political group connected to Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi, according to a 2016 Washington Post report. At the time, Bondi’s office was considering complaints concerning Trump University; her office later did not pursue the matter. The foundation had initially reported the payment as a donation to a Kansas charity with a similar name, though that charity did not receive the money. After the error was raised, the foundation corrected its tax filing and paid a $2,500 penalty. A Trump Organization official said the foundation reimbursed itself, and the foundation acknowledged that the payment was an illegal political contribution. These facts establish a prohibited contribution and its timing alongside the office’s review. They do not establish that Trump paid Bondi personally, that Bondi agreed to exchange official action for the payment, or that the contribution caused her office’s decision. The payment’s connection to Bondi’s political network and the pending complaints raised questions about the foundation’s compliance with rules barring political contributions by charities. The available reporting supports describing the payment as illegal, but it does not prove the quid pro quo asserted by the original headline.

title: Donald Trump and Roger Stone weigh the possibility of a gubernatorial race
description_medium: In late 2013 and early 2014, Trump considered running for New York governor against Andrew Cuomo. Political consultant Michael Caputo pressed Trump adviser Roger Stone for a meeting to make the case. Stone viewed Cuomo as a formidable opponent and reportedly thought the governorship was too small a job for Trump. Trump never entered the race.
description_long: Donald Trump considered challenging New York Governor Andrew Cuomo in the 2014 election. Two state assemblymen and political consultant Michael Caputo encouraged a run and prepared a memo arguing that the governorship could be a stepping stone to the presidency. The memo drew Trump’s interest, and Caputo pressed Trump’s political adviser Roger Stone to meet and make the case. Stone saw a statewide race against Cuomo as difficult for a Republican in a heavily Democratic state. He described Cuomo as well-funded and a tough opponent, and said the job was too small for Trump, who would dislike living in Albany. Trump publicly criticized Cuomo but did not become a candidate. The episode was part of Trump’s early political maneuvering before his 2016 presidential campaign: the governor’s race offered a possible route into elected office, while his advisers disagreed about whether it was viable. The record describes a serious possibility discussed among Trump’s allies, not a declared campaign or a formal bid.

title: Supreme Court allows Hobby Lobby companies to claim a religious exemption under RFRA
description_medium: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. (2014), the Supreme Court held that closely held for-profit corporations could claim protection under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act against the federal contraceptive-coverage rule at issue. The ruling addressed a specific statutory dispute. It did not give corporations every right held by individuals, as the timeline headline suggests.
description_long: On June 30, 2014, the Supreme Court decided Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., a challenge to the Affordable Care Act’s contraceptive-coverage requirement. The Court held that the closely held for-profit companies before it could invoke the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), and that applying the requirement to them violated that statute. The decision concerned the companies’ religious objections and the federal government’s chosen means of providing coverage; it did not declare that corporations possess every constitutional or human right held by individuals. The majority explained its decision through RFRA’s statutory protections and the specific claims made by the companies. The ruling was significant because it recognized that closely held corporations could exercise religion for purposes of that statute, while the dissent warned about extending religious-liberty protections into commercial activity. The holding remained tied to the contraceptive-coverage mandate and to the companies before the Court. It was not a general ruling that corporations and individuals have identical rights.
